newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on weak technology sector; Greenspan effect.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on weak technology sector; Greenspan effect.

text.p: Stocks fell sharply Thursday amid a sell-off in technology shares and leftover pressure from Wednesday's warning by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan over the market's lofty levels.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 58.11 points at 6,925.07, for a two-day loss of more than 100 points.

But the Dow's stiff losses paled in comparison to the technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index's fall of 27.89 points to 1,312.66. It was the steepest one-day decline on Nasdaq since last July 23's drop of 32.32 points.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,601 to 896 on active volume of 464 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Rising interest rates in the bond market again posed a problem for stocks.

The closely watched 30-year Treasury bond was off 13/32, which raised its yield to 6.81 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.78 percent as jitters over Greenspan's blunt comments on interest rates pressed on the bond market.
The heightened sense of caution in the stock market was felt most heavily in the technology arena, where investors were clearly rethinking the group's price levels.

"There is a fundamental valuation change occurring," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The communications equipment makers in particular are being revalued and the valuations are going down."

The selling pressure on tech stocks -- a group that has performed unimpressively in recent weeks -- appeared to reach a flashpoint with news late Wednesday of the mega-merger between network equipment makers U.S. Robotics Corp. and 3Com Corp.
Opinions on Wall Street about the $6.6 billion merger varied but most telling for the networking group, some analysts said, was what they described as the low price 3Com is paying for U.S. Robotics.

"If anything, this deal is more of a take-under than a takeover," said Salomon Brothers analyst Peter Swartz. "This deal says the days of the 35 to 40 percent premiums paid in previous networking acquisitions are over."
The stock of 3Com fell four points to 35 and U.S. Robotics lost 1-7/8 to 59-1/8.

The bearishness spread to other networking stocks. Among them, Ascend Communications Inc. lost 5-3/8 to 57, Cascade Communications Corp., fell 2-1/2 to 30-1/8 and Cisco Systems Inc. sank 3-1/16 to 55-1/16.
The broad selling quickly drew in other computer-related groups. Intel Corp. tumbled 6-41/64 to 139-47/64 and Microsoft Corp. slid 4-1/8 to 96-1/8.
Despite the more guarded atmosphere on Wall Street, some analysts welcomed the market's retreat.

"This is healthier than what we would have seen if the market had continued blindly higher," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "The market has tended to get a little ahead of itself and I think we're seeing a reassessment, not a great big correction."
In individual issues, Centennial Technologies Inc. extended its wild run, plunging 11-1/4 to 3-1/2 after saying restatements to its earnings would show it lost money for the last three years.
The shares have vacillated wildly since the arrest of the Centennial's founder and fired chief executive, Emanuel Pinez, earlier this month.
Citrix Systems Inc. tumbled 15-5/8 to 10-5/8 after the company warned late Wednesday it could face increased competition from Microsoft Corp.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 10.61 points to 795.07. The American Stock Exchange index was off 2.15 to 595.16.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 4.25 to 417.89. The average share was down 44 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,602.591, down 89.664, or 1.17 percent.
